About.title: About Trillion
About.slogan: An eye for stocks — for everyone.
About.sub: Every lens, as data — the judgment is yours.
About.problemBody: Investment information is scattered, and the market is loud with predictions and tips. Chat rooms sell you "the stock that will go up"; paid tools hide their method inside a black box. In between, individuals end up leaning on what someone else says. The problem is not too little information — it is the lack of a tool to read it with your own eyes. When someone sells you a stock with great confidence, the first thing to look at is not the confidence — it is their incentive.
About.lensTitle: The TR-AI Lens — how we read a stock
About.lensIntro: We read one stock through several proven methods, each on its own. Every lens answers just one honest question, and writes down — right on the screen — which metrics it uses and whose research it leans on.

lens.momentum: Momentum — is the trend continuing? (trend persistence)
lens.value: Value — is it cheap against earnings and assets? (the value investing pioneered by Benjamin Graham · the value premium Fama & French established in the data)
lens.quality: Quality — how well does it turn assets into profit? (Novy-Marx 2013 · gross profits ÷ assets)
lens.fscore: F-Score — is the balance sheet weak? (Piotroski 2000 · a 9-point financial-health checklist)
lens.lowvol: Low Volatility — steady per unit of risk? (the low-volatility anomaly)
lens.extra: Asset Growth · Technical — over-investment and overheating signals. (RSI — Wilder 1978 · moving averages)

About.lensClose: Nothing is hidden. Not a black box — a lens we open. Each lens shows the numbers behind it, and when the data is not there, that lens simply says "insufficient data."
About.noRecTitle: We do not predict, and we do not recommend
About.noRecBody: There is no "buy this stock" signal here. A lens hands you evidence, not certainty; material, not a conclusion. We set several proven viewpoints side by side — the decision to buy or sell is entirely yours. A good tool does not make the call for you. It only helps you make a better one.
About.coverageBody: Korea · United States · Japan · China · Vietnam · United Kingdom — six markets. For each, we take first-hand material — prices, news, filings — from public sources and show it as it is. We do not invent values. And when the data looks odd, we do not erase it on a hunch.
About.step1: Pick a stock, read the lenses. See at a glance how one stock reads through momentum, value, quality, financial health, and more — each on its own.
About.step2: Read the disagreement. When the lenses disagree is the most important signal — cheap but weak, or pricey but sturdy?
About.step3: You make the call. The material is gathered; the conclusion is yours. We do not press the button for you.
About.quote: “The best thing a human being can do is to help another human being know more.”
About.disclaimer: Trillion does not trade, broker, or advise on financial products, and does not intermediate any transaction. The information Trillion provides is for reference only and is not a solicitation or advice to invest.

EtfLens.etnBody: This product is an ETN (exchange-traded note). The issuing brokerage contracts to pay the return of an underlying index, so it is a strategy product and, unlike an ETF, it has no individual holdings (basket). The product name carries the issuer, the tracked index, and the type (leveraged or inverse).
EtfLens.etnWarn: ⚠️ An ETN carries the credit risk of its issuer.
EtfLens.etnWarnLeveraged: Leveraged and inverse types track a multiple of, or the opposite of, the underlying index, so their value can erode when held for a long time (volatility decay).

fscore.detailsBasis: ▾ Scoring basis · origin · why we call it financial health
fscore.howToReadBody: In practice it is usually read as <s>7 or above good · 4 to 6 middling · 0 to 3 weak</s>. It is the sum of the nine signals Piotroski devised (the higher, the sturdier).
fscore.whyFinHealthBody: The accounting scholar Piotroski built it in 2000 to <s>screen out the genuinely distressed</s> among cheap value stocks. In our broad sample and 12-year backtest, however, the score showed no valid relationship with subsequent returns (t≈0.7). So we use it only as a reading of <s>financial health</s>, never as a return forecast — that is why this lens is graded financial health.

StockLens.intro: We show how proven methods each read this stock. Not a buy or sell signal — material for you to judge for yourself.
StockLens.readingGuideSummary: ▾ How to read this screen · confidence grades
StockLens.readingGuide: Every card carries a confidence grade — Verified means the return signal itself was confirmed, Weak signal means it is famous but weak in our data, Reference shows state only, and Financial health is financial strength, not a return signal. Tap a lens to unfold why it reads that way.

StockLens.closingAllPos: Whether short- or long-term, the methods read mostly positive.
StockLens.closingAllWarn: Whether short- or long-term, the methods read mostly negative.
StockLens.closingLongPosShortWarn: Long-horizon methods read it favorably, short-horizon methods unfavorably — the read splits by time horizon.

StockLens.narrativeCutoffMomentum: Cutoff: above {hi}% is classified up, below {lo}% is classified down.
StockLens.narrativeMethodMomentum: 12-1 momentum ranks the market by the trailing 12-month return, excluding the most recent month. Jegadeesh and Titman first showed this in the data in 1993.
StockLens.narrativeStock: This stock ranks in the top {pct}%, read as “{verdict}.”
StockLens.narrativeMethodLowvol: The low-volatility lens measures stability via the trailing one-year annualized volatility of daily returns. It rests on the low-volatility anomaly (BAB) — calmer stocks tending to do better per unit of risk.
StockLens.narrativeCutoffLowvol: Cutoff: below {lo}% annualized volatility is classified calm, above {hi}% is classified jumpy.
StockLens.narrativeMethodValuation: The value lens checks whether the price looks cheap or expensive next to earnings (PER). It traces to value investing as practiced by Benjamin Graham, with Fama and French establishing the value premium in the data.
StockLens.narrativeCutoffValuation: Cutoff: PER below {lo} is classified low, above {hi} is classified high.
StockLens.narrativeMethodQuality: The quality lens measures profit efficiency via gross profit over total assets (GP/A). Novy-Marx first showed this in the data in 2013.
StockLens.narrativeCutoffQuality: Cutoff: GP/A above {hi}% is classified high, below {lo}% is classified low.
StockLens.narrativeMethodAssetgrowth: The asset growth lens tracks how fast total assets grew versus a year ago. Cooper, Gulen, and Schill first showed this in the data in 2008 — it is also the investment factor (CMA) in the Fama-French five-factor model.
StockLens.narrativeCutoffAssetgrowth: Cutoff: asset growth below {lo}% is classified conservative, above {hi}% is classified aggressive.
StockLens.narrativeMethodTechnical: The technical lens reads overbought/oversold via 14-day RSI, and trend via position relative to the 200-day moving average. RSI was created by Welles Wilder in 1978.
StockLens.narrativeCutoffTechnical: Cutoff: RSI above {hi} is classified overbought, below {lo} is classified oversold.
StockLens.narrativeStockTechnical: It is currently {pct}% versus the 200-day average, read as “{verdict}.”
StockLens.narrativeMethodFscore: The F-Score counts whether 9 checks on profitability, financial stability, and efficiency improved from a year ago. Piotroski first showed this in the data in 2000.
StockLens.narrativeStockFscore: This stock scores {score}/{max}, in the “{band}” band (see the 9 checks above).
